quiz.circleTapKey: Tap the key on the circle.
quiz.circleTritone: The tritone substitute sits directly opposite the dominant on the circle.
quiz.circleSubvResolve: Find the original dominant on the opposite side — it resolves one step counter-clockwise.
quiz.circleDominant: The dominant sits one step clockwise from the chord it leads to.
quiz.circleResolve: A dominant resolves one step counter-clockwise.
quiz.circleColtrane: The cycle splits the circle into three equal parts: each next key is four steps counter-clockwise.
quiz.circleFrame251: Inside a key's frame: V is the major chord one step clockwise from the tonic, ii is the minor chord on the opposite side of the frame.
quiz.circlePivot: The shared chords are where the frames of both keys overlap.
quiz.circleBorrowed: Borrowed chords sit in the second, blue frame (three steps counter-clockwise) — that is the parallel minor.
quiz.fretCountDegrees: Count scale degrees upward from the highlighted root: the root is 1.
quiz.fretStackThirds: A chord is built from every other note of the scale: root, third, fifth, seventh.
quiz.fretChordInScale: On the fretboard: the key's scale, with the chord's notes highlighted.
quiz.fretChordRoot: On the fretboard: the key's scale, with the chord's root highlighted.
quiz.fretChordOnC: On the fretboard: this chord built from C.
quiz.circleTap: Tap the key on the circle. Count steps from C: clockwise adds sharps, counter-clockwise adds flats.
quiz.circleRead: The key is marked on the circle. Steps clockwise from C are sharps (in order F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯, A♯, E♯), counter-clockwise are flats (in order B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭, C♭).

loop.markAfterLoop: The button unlocks after a full pass of the progression.
loop.micWindowHint: Play the target note on the downbeat of the new chord — the first beat is checked. Headphones work best, so the mic does not hear the backing.
loop.micError: Microphone unavailable — use the self-mark button.
loop.allVariants: To pass the exercise, every variant needs its own successful loops.
loop.transposedNotice: The goal and chord hints refer to the original key ({{key}}). Chords, fretboard and mic targets are transposed.
loop.fretboardLegend: Numbers are chord degrees; the root (1) is a solid marker (ringed when it is a mic target).

goals.targetThird: Land on the chord's third at each change — Am→C, C→E, Em→G, D→F#.
goals.targetFifth: Land on the chord's fifth — Am→E, C→G, Em→B, D→A.
goals.voiceLeading: Before the change, play the common tone or a step next to a note of the next chord (Gm→Bbm: shared Bb; Gm→Cm: shared G).
goals.switchingKeys: Halfway through the loop the key moves from G to B — shift your lines (scales/arpeggios) to the new key.
goals.tritoneNormal: Resolve G7 to C — the third of G7 (B) rises a half step to C, the seventh (F) falls a half step to E.
goals.tritoneSubV: Over Db7 emphasize the third (F) and the seventh (Cb = B), then resolve them by half step: F→E, B→C.
goals.secondaryDominants: After each secondary dominant, land on the third of the next chord.
goals.borrowedBackdoor: Over Fm7 play F dorian, over Bb7 play Bb Lydian dominant (or Bb mixolydian), then step into a chord tone of C.
goals.triads: Play only triads over the loop — move each chord to its closest inversion instead of jumping shapes.
goals.pentatonicBox1: Improvise using box 1 only (frets 5–8) — your first real improvisation.
goals.majorC: Phrase with the C major scale and end your lines on the note C.
goals.pentatonicBoxes: With each loop, move to the neighbouring pentatonic box.
goals.modeCharacteristic: Emphasize the mode's characteristic note over the backing.
goals.pentThenMode: Play four bars with the minor pentatonic only, then for the next four add the two notes that turn it into Dorian. Listen to what changes.
goals.approachBelow: Just before the chord changes, play the note a half step below the new chord's root and land on the root on beat one: G#→A, B→C, D#→E, C#→D.
goals.approachBelowLabel: Level 5: a half step from below
goals.approachEnclosure: Surround the target: a half step above, a half step below, the root on beat one: Bb–G#→A, Db–B→C, F–D#→E, Eb–C#→D.
goals.approachThirdBelow: Approach the third of each chord from a half step below and land on it on beat one: E→F (Dm7), A#→B (G7), D#→E (Cmaj7).
goals.approachThirdEnclosure: Surround the third: Gb–E→F (Dm7), C–A#→B (G7), F–D#→E (Cmaj7).
goals.limitThreeNotes: Play with only three notes of box 1: A, C and D. All your attention goes to rhythm and phrase length.
goals.limitOneString: Play on the G string only: A minor pentatonic sits there on frets 0, 2, 5, 7, 9 and 12. The phrase comes from moving along the neck.
goals.limitRhythm: Play every phrase with the same rhythm: a quarter note, two eighths, a half note. Change the notes, keep the rhythm.
goals.bluesMinorPent: Play the whole blues with the minor pentatonic from the key's root. It sounds raw because its minor third rubs against the dominant chord.
goals.bluesMajorPent: Play the whole blues with the major pentatonic: the same box shape three frets lower. It sounds brighter because it has the chord's major third.
goals.bluesMixedPent: Change colour with the chord: major pentatonic over the I chord, minor over IV and V.
goals.pedalModes: The root stays in the bass and the variant changes the mode. Play slowly and rest on the notes that set this mode apart from the others.
goals.chordScaleCharacteristic: On every chord, play its characteristic tone from the hinted scale.
goals.arpeggiosOnly: Play chord arpeggios only — outline the harmony.
goals.targetRoot: Land on the chord's root at each change — Am→A, C→C, Em→E, D→D.
goals.targetSeventh: Land on the chord's seventh — Am7→G, Cmaj7→B, Em7→D, D7→C.
goals.targetAny: No fixed target: land on any chord tone you hear — your first free improvisation.
goals.voiceLeadingThirdsSevenths: Voice the thirds and sevenths smoothly: F→F→E or C→B→B through Dm7–G7–Cmaj7.
goals.switchingKeysEasy: Halfway through the loop the key moves from C to F major. One note changes (B becomes Bb) — switch scales when the hint shows the new key.
goals.tritoneVideo: Chromatic bass descent: Bm7–Bb7–Am7–Ab7–Gmaj7. Bb7 and Ab7 are tritone substitutes of the dominants.
goals.borrowedDiatonic: The diatonic road to C: Dm7–G7. Compare its sound with the backdoor.
goals.melodicMinor67: Emphasize the 6 (F#) and the major 7 (G#) over both Am chords.
goals.melodicMinorHints: Use the melodic-minor hint shown on each chord.
goals.harmonicMinorGSharp: Over E7 emphasize G# — the characteristic note of A harmonic minor.
goals.harmonicMinorPhrygian: Over E7 play E Phrygian dominant (from A harmonic minor).
goals.giantStepsRoots: Play chord roots through the whole 16-bar form.
goals.giantStepsPattern: Play a 1-2-3-5 pattern of each chord through the form.
goals.giantStepsArps: Play chord arpeggios through the whole form.
goals.bluesBox1: 12-bar blues in A — improvise in pentatonic box 1.
goals.bluesChordTones: 12-bar blues in A — land on a chord tone at every change.
goals.playRest: Play only in bars marked “play”. In “rest” bars play nothing: listen to the backing and plan the next phrase.
goals.callResponse: Two bars of question, two bars of answer. Start the answer with a motif from the question and end it on a chord tone.
goals.playRestLabel: Play a bar, rest a bar

e-string-notes.name: Notes of the E string
e-string-notes.theory: Improvisation starts with knowing the fretboard. Step one is the low E string (6th string): from fret 0 to 12 the notes run chromatically — E F F# G G# A A# B C C# D D# E. Once you know it by heart, you can find the root of a scale or chord quickly, because most shapes start on this string. Practice both directions: see a fret and name the note, then read a name and find the fret.

key-signatures.name: Key Signatures
key-signatures.theory: A key tells you which notes “live at home”. The circle of fifths orders the keys: moving clockwise adds sharps (C→G→D→A→E→B), counter-clockwise adds flats (C→F→Bb→Eb→Ab). Accidentals always join in the same order (sharps: F#, C#, G#, D#…; flats: Bb, Eb, Ab, Db…), so a key's position on the circle tells you at once which notes are altered. When a bandmate says “play in D”, the key signature is what makes that unambiguous. In improvisation this is step one: the key signature tells you which seven notes you can build a solo from in a given tune.

pentatonic-scale.name: Pentatonic Scale
pentatonic-scale.theory: The minor pentatonic (1 b3 4 5 b7) is most players’ first improvising language: it sounds right in blues, rock and folk. Box 1 (e.g. A minor at frets 5–8) sits comfortably under the fingers, so you can focus on phrasing instead of finding notes. Box 2 starts on the minor third and extends the scale up the neck. Switch keys with the selector: the shape stays the same and just slides along the neck. Play with a metronome, up and down, evenly in time. Every box is made of two shapes that alternate: a rectangle (two adjacent strings, notes 3 frets apart) and a stack (three adjacent strings, 2 frets apart); between the G and B strings everything shifts by one fret. The idea comes from the Fret Science lesson “Two Simple Shapes UNLOCK the Pentatonic Scale”.

major-scale.name: Major Scale
major-scale.theory: The major scale (1 2 3 4 5 6 7) is the reference point for everything that follows: modes, chord construction and harmony are all described against it. A one-position box, two or three notes per string, lays the whole scale out as a repeatable pattern. Play it up and down with a metronome, then in thirds and fourths — that is when the scale starts sounding like melody rather than an exercise.

fretboard-notes.name: Notes of the Rest of the Fretboard
fretboard-notes.term: Notes of the Rest of the Fretboard
fretboard-notes.theory: Now you extend the map to every string. Neighbouring strings E–A–D–G–B are a perfect fourth apart (5 semitones), with one exception: G to B is a major third (4 semitones). So the note at fret 5 of one string is the next open string (on the G string, fret 4). The goal is to see every note anywhere in frets 1–12; without that, following the changes higher up the neck is guesswork.

pentatonic-positions.name: Pentatonic Scale Positions
pentatonic-positions.theory: The five boxes are one scale — G minor pentatonic (G, Bb, C, D, F) — spread over the whole neck. Each box starts on the next note of that scale. The video names the boxes after their starting note: G minor pent (fret 3), Bb major pent (fret 5), C dorian pent (fret 7), D phrygian pent (fret 10), F mixolydian pent (fret 12). Every box uses the same five notes; only the shape under your fingers changes. Learn the boxes one by one, then connect neighbours.

modes.name: Modes
modes.theory: Modes are the seven scales you get by starting the major scale on each degree: I Ionian, II Dorian, III Phrygian, IV Lydian, V Mixolydian, VI Aeolian, VII Locrian. Compared with the major scale on the same root, Dorian has b3 and b7, Phrygian b2 b3 b6 b7, Lydian #4, Mixolydian b7, Aeolian b3 b6 b7 and Locrian b2 b3 b5 b6 b7. Each mode has a characteristic note that sets it apart from plain major or minor: the major sixth in Dorian, b2 in Phrygian, #4 in Lydian, b7 in Mixolydian. Emphasize those notes when you want the mode to be heard. A practical shortcut: a mode is a pentatonic from the same root plus two notes (Fret Science lesson “Stop Memorizing Modes”).

chord-construction.name: How Chords Are Built
chord-construction.theory: Chords come from the scale: stack every other note (1-3-5) from a scale degree. In F major: F-A-C is degree I (major), G-Bb-D is ii (minor), E-G-Bb is vii (diminished). You recognize a triad type by its distances: major third + perfect fifth = major, minor third + perfect fifth = minor, minor third + diminished fifth = dim, major third + augmented fifth = aug. The same stacking extends to seventh chords and every extension used in improvisation.

chord-scale-major.name: Chord/Scale Relationships (Major)
chord-scale-major.theory: Every chord in a key has “its” mode. In C major: Cmaj7 → Ionian, Dm7 → Dorian (Dm13 is the same chord with extensions), Em7 → Phrygian, Fmaj7 → Lydian (hence the #11 in Fmaj7#11), G7 → Mixolydian, Am7 → Aeolian, Bm7b5 → Locrian. In practice you play the notes of the key, but on each chord you aim at its characteristic note. This is the first step from “playing in the key” to “following the changes”.

triads.name: Triads
triads.theory: Triads on the top three strings (G-B-E) are the most economical way to see harmony on the neck. Each chord has three inversions sitting next to each other, so a chord change means moving your fingers a fret or two. The same shapes work for comping and as targets for melodic lines. Also drill the intervals: major 1 3 5, minor 1 b3 5, diminished 1 b3 b5, augmented 1 3 #5.

arpeggios.name: Arpeggios
arpeggios.theory: An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time. It contains only chord tones, so it always fits over that chord — the safest material when chords keep changing. The diagrams show each arpeggio across all six strings in one position: 1 b3 5 b7 for m7, 1 3 5 b7 for the dominant 7, 1 3 5 7 for maj7 and 1 b3 b5 b7 for m7b5. The arpeggio is the skeleton of a line; scale notes, chromatics and passing notes go around it.

target-chord-tones.name: How to Target Chord Tones
target-chord-tones.theory: “Following the changes” starts with landing on a chord tone exactly when the chord changes. Over Am–C–Em–D work through four levels: roots first, then thirds (C, E, G, F#), fifths (E, G, B, A) and sevenths. The third tells you whether the chord is major or minor, the fifth sounds stable, the seventh adds colour. Start the line on the previous chord and finish it on the new one — that is what makes an improvisation audibly follow the harmony.

voice-leading.name: Voice Leading
voice-leading.theory: Voice leading means moving between chords by the shortest path: through a common tone or by a half or whole step. Gm and Bbm share Bb, and the D of Gm falls a half step to the Db of Bbm — the move shown in the video. Gm and Cm share G. Play that note right before the change and the line glides into the new chord instead of jumping. In a ii–V–I (Dm7–G7–Cmaj7) the shortest path runs through the thirds and sevenths: F→F→E and C→B→B.

switching-keys.name: How to Switch Keys While Improvising
switching-keys.term: How to Switch Keys While Improvising
switching-keys.theory: When a tune changes key, your scales and arpeggios have to change with it. A chord shared by both keys (pivot chord) or a ii–V that introduces the new key helps. Start with the easy move from C to F major, where only one note differs (B becomes Bb), then move on to G to B major. Work in this order: hear the change, pick the shape in the new key, then connect both keys with one line.

tritone-subs.name: Tritone Substitutions
tritone-subs.theory: A tritone substitution replaces a dominant chord with the dominant a tritone away: G7 → Db7. Both chords share the same tritone (B and F in G7, F and Cb = B in Db7), so they lead to the same chord, but the bass now moves chromatically: Dm7–Db7–Cmaj7 instead of Dm7–G7–Cmaj7. Over Db7 emphasize the third and seventh and resolve them by half step. The video shows the mechanism in Bm7–Bb7–Am7–Ab7–Gmaj7.

secondary-dominants.name: Secondary Dominants
secondary-dominants.theory: A secondary dominant is a dominant chord (V7) that briefly treats another chord of the key as its tonic. In C major: A7 leads to Dm7 (V7/ii), B7 to Em7, C7 to Fmaj7, D7 to G7, E7 to Am7; the video’s table adds G7 → Cmaj7, the regular dominant. Secondary dominants add tension and motion without changing the key. In Cmaj7–A7–Dm7–G7 each dominant leads to the next chord, and you hear it most clearly when you land on the target chord’s third.

borrowed-chords.name: Borrowed Chords
borrowed-chords.theory: Borrowed chords come from the parallel minor key. In C major you borrow them from C minor: Fm (iv), Bb7 (bVII7), Ab (bVI) and Eb (bIII). The best-known case is the backdoor ii–V: Fm7–Bb7–Cmaj7. Over Fm7 play F dorian, over Bb7 play Bb Lydian dominant or Bb mixolydian. The Bb bass rises a whole step into C, and that move is the “back door” sound.

melodic-minor.name: Melodic Minor Scale and Modes
melodic-minor.theory: The melodic minor scale (1 2 b3 4 5 6 7) is a minor scale with a major sixth and seventh: minor at the bottom, major on top. For improvisation it is more useful than harmonic minor, because its modes supply the scales for m(maj7), 7alt, 7#11 and other typical jazz sounds. Start with the A melodic minor box around fret 4, then play the next position up, and move both shapes to other keys with the selector.

chord-scale-melodic.name: Melodic Minor Chord/Scale Relationships
chord-scale-melodic.theory: Each mode of melodic minor fits a different chord: I melodic minor → m(maj7), II Dorian b2 → m7 (sus b9), III Lydian augmented → maj7#5, IV Lydian dominant → 7#11, V Mixolydian b6 → 7b13, VI Aeolian b5 (Locrian ♮2) → m7b5, VII Altered → 7alt. The video also pairs Altered with m7b5; usually, though, it is played over 7alt. When you see a chord symbol, you know which melodic minor to take the scale from: over G7alt you play Ab melodic minor.

harmonic-minor.name: Harmonic Minor Scale and Modes
harmonic-minor.theory: The harmonic minor scale (1 2 b3 4 5 b6 7) has a characteristic step and a half between b6 and 7 that gives it its “exotic” sound. It sits near the end of the learning order not because it is hard, but because it matters less for improvisation than everything before it. It is used most over the dominant of a minor key (E7 in A minor), where it brings out G#. Learn the C harmonic minor box around fret 6, then the next position up, and move both shapes to other keys.

chord-scale-harmonic.name: Harmonic Minor Chord/Scale Relationships
chord-scale-harmonic.theory: The modes of harmonic minor and their chords: I harmonic minor → m(maj7), II Locrian #6 → m7b5, III Ionian #5 → maj7#5, IV Dorian #4 → m7, V Phrygian dominant → 7, VI Lydian #2 → maj7, VII Superlocrian bb7 → dim7. In practice you will reach for Phrygian dominant most: over a V7 leading to a minor chord (E7 → Am) it brings b9 and b13, which pull towards the resolution. The other modes come up less often, but it pays to recognize their chord symbols.

giant-steps.name: Giant Steps
giant-steps.theory: John Coltrane’s “Giant Steps” closes the list. The key moves down by major thirds (B → G → Eb), often with a new chord every two beats. Each new key is introduced by its dominant (D7 → G, Bb7 → Eb, F#7 → B) or by a ii–V (Am7–D7, Fm7–Bb7, C#m7–F#7). Practice the whole 16-bar form in three steps: roots only, then a 1-2-3-5 pattern on each chord, finally arpeggios. Start at 60 BPM; once you get through the form without getting lost, all the earlier modules come together into one system.

e-string-notes.e1.name: Practice: position → note (E string)
e-string-notes.e1.desc: Open the “fretboard → note” practice on the E string, frets 1–12. Every position needs at least 3 answers and 80% accuracy.

e-string-notes.e2.name: Practice: note → position (E string)
e-string-notes.e2.desc: The reverse direction: read a note name and point to it in the tab. It uses the same position stats as the previous exercise. Extra practice — not required to pass the module.

key-signatures.e1.name: Quiz: notes of the key
key-signatures.e1.desc: Which notes make up a key and which of them are raised or lowered. The key is marked on the circle of fifths, and after you answer the circle shows its chords.

key-signatures.e2.name: Note in the key
key-signatures.e2.desc: The decision you make in a solo: you play in the given key and pick the note that belongs to it, for example G or G#.

pentatonic-scale.e1.name: Diagram: minor pentatonic, box 1
pentatonic-scale.e1.desc: Box 1 of the minor pentatonic (A minor by default, frets 5–8). The selector changes the key and the shape slides along the neck. A run is the whole scale up and down. The colours show how the box is built: a rectangle (two strings, notes 3 frets apart) and a stack (three strings, 2 frets apart). The “View” switch adds the blue note, the second, or marks the notes to bend.

pentatonic-scale.e2.name: Diagram: minor pentatonic, box 2
pentatonic-scale.e2.desc: Box 2, starting on the minor third (frets 7–10 in A minor). It connects to box 1 and extends the scale up the neck.

major-scale.e1.name: Diagram: major scale, lower position
major-scale.e1.desc: The major scale in one position (A major, frets 2–6). Use the selector to move it to other keys.

major-scale.e2.name: Diagram: major scale, higher position
major-scale.e2.desc: The same scale in the next position (C major, frets 7–11).

fretboard-notes.e1.name: Practice: position → note (whole neck)
fretboard-notes.e1.desc: Open the “fretboard → note” practice on all strings, frets 1–12. Every position needs at least 3 answers and 80% accuracy.

fretboard-notes.e2.name: Practice: note → position (whole neck)
fretboard-notes.e2.desc: The reverse direction across the neck. It uses the same position stats as the previous exercise. Extra practice — not required to pass the module.

pentatonic-positions.e1.name: Box 1: from G (fret 3)
pentatonic-positions.e1.desc: Box 1 of G minor pentatonic, frets 3–6.

pentatonic-positions.e2.name: Box 2: from Bb (fret 5)
pentatonic-positions.e2.desc: Box 2 of the same scale, starting on Bb — “Bb major pent” in the video. Frets 5–8.

pentatonic-positions.e3.name: Box 3: from C (fret 7)
pentatonic-positions.e3.desc: Box 3, starting on C — “C dorian pent” in the video. Frets 7–11.

pentatonic-positions.e4.name: Box 4: from D (fret 10)
pentatonic-positions.e4.desc: Box 4, starting on D — “D phrygian pent” in the video. Frets 10–13.

pentatonic-positions.e5.name: Box 5: from F (fret 12)
pentatonic-positions.e5.desc: Box 5, starting on F — “F mixolydian pent” in the video. Frets 12–15.

modes.e1.name: Quiz: modes
modes.e1.desc: The characteristic note of a mode on the fretboard, a mode's notes from a given root, the parent scale on the circle, and recognizing modes by ear.

modes.e2.name: Characteristic note on the fretboard
modes.e2.desc: Find the note that gives a mode its sound: 6 in Dorian, #4 in Lydian, b7 in Mixolydian.

chord-construction.e1.name: Quiz: chords from the scale
chord-construction.e1.desc: Build a chord on a degree of the major scale: tap its notes on the fretboard and name its type — triads and seventh chords.

chord-construction.e2.name: Build the chord on the fretboard
chord-construction.e2.desc: The chord's root is highlighted. Tap its third, fifth or seventh — every other note of the scale.

chord-scale-major.e1.name: Chord → mode (major)
chord-scale-major.e1.desc: Dm7 → Dorian, Fmaj7 → Lydian, G7 → Mixolydian…

chord-scale-major.e2.name: Characteristic note over the chord
chord-scale-major.e2.desc: For a chord in a key, tap the characteristic note of the matching mode — the one worth resting a phrase on.

triads.e1.name: Loop: triads over Am–C–Em–D
triads.e1.desc: Play only triads over the loop, moving each inversion by the smallest finger movement. 2 successful loops.

triads.e2.name: Name → intervals
triads.e2.desc: Major 1 3 5, minor 1 b3 5, dim, aug + seventh chords.

arpeggios.e1.name: Diagram: m7 arpeggio
arpeggios.e1.desc: Cm7 arpeggio (1 b3 5 b7) across all strings, frets 8–12.

arpeggios.e2.name: Diagram: 7 (dominant) arpeggio
arpeggios.e2.desc: G7 arpeggio (1 3 5 b7) across all strings, frets 3–7.

target-chord-tones.e1.name: Loop: roots, thirds, fifths, sevenths
target-chord-tones.e1.desc: Am–C–Em–D in four levels. Land on the given chord tone at every change; each level needs its own successful loops.

target-chord-tones.e2.name: Loop: any chord tone
target-chord-tones.e2.desc: The same progression with no fixed target — land on any chord tone.

voice-leading.e1.name: Loop: Gm → Bbm
voice-leading.e1.desc: Before the change play the common tone (Bb) or a neighbouring step.

voice-leading.e2.name: Loop: Gm → Cm
voice-leading.e2.desc: Common tone: G. Minimize finger movement.

switching-keys.e1.name: Quiz: common chords and ii–V
switching-keys.e1.desc: Pivot chords between keys and the ii–V that announces a key.

switching-keys.e2.name: Loop: C major → F major
switching-keys.e2.desc: The easier change — one note differs (B becomes Bb).

tritone-subs.e1.name: Quiz: tritone substitutions
tritone-subs.e1.desc: subV for G7? V for a subV? subV→I resolution.

tritone-subs.e2.name: Loop: G7 and Db7
tritone-subs.e2.desc: Three variants: a plain ii–V–I, the same progression with Db7 and the video’s chain. Each variant needs its own successful loops.

secondary-dominants.e1.name: Quiz: secondary dominants
secondary-dominants.e1.desc: Find the secondary dominant of a chord in the key and the chord it leads to — in every major key.

secondary-dominants.e2.name: Loop: secondary dominants
secondary-dominants.e2.desc: Two variants: Cmaj7–A7–Dm7–G7 and a progression with five dominants. After each dominant, land on the third of the next chord.

borrowed-chords.e1.name: Quiz: borrowed chords
borrowed-chords.e1.desc: Name the degree of a chord borrowed from the parallel minor and recognize the backdoor progression.

borrowed-chords.e2.name: Loop: ii–V–I and backdoor
borrowed-chords.e2.desc: Two variants leading to Cmaj7: Dm7–G7 and Fm7–Bb7. Compare how they sound.

melodic-minor.e1.name: Diagram: A melodic minor, lower position
melodic-minor.e1.desc: The scale 1 2 b3 4 5 6 7 at frets 3–7. Use the selector to move it to other keys.

melodic-minor.e2.name: Diagram: A melodic minor, higher position
melodic-minor.e2.desc: The next position of the same scale, frets 7–11.

chord-scale-melodic.e1.name: Quiz: melodic minor modes
chord-scale-melodic.e1.desc: Chord → mode, mode → chord and the parent scale of a specific chord.

chord-scale-melodic.e2.name: Quiz: which melodic minor?
chord-scale-melodic.e2.desc: For a chord (e.g. D7#11), name the melodic minor its scale comes from.

harmonic-minor.e1.name: Diagram: C harmonic minor, lower position
harmonic-minor.e1.desc: The scale 1 2 b3 4 5 b6 7 at frets 5–9. Use the selector to move it to other keys.

harmonic-minor.e2.name: Diagram: C harmonic minor, higher position
harmonic-minor.e2.desc: The next position of the same scale, frets 10–14.

chord-scale-harmonic.e1.name: Quiz: harmonic minor modes
chord-scale-harmonic.e1.desc: Chord → mode, mode → chord and the parent scale of a specific chord.

chord-scale-harmonic.e2.name: Quiz: which harmonic minor?
chord-scale-harmonic.e2.desc: For a chord (e.g. E7), name the harmonic minor its scale comes from.

giant-steps.e1.name: Quiz: the Coltrane cycle
giant-steps.e1.desc: Key order, the dominants and ii–Vs leading to B, G and Eb, and the cycle moved to other keys.

giant-steps.e2.name: Loop: Giant Steps
giant-steps.e2.desc: The whole 16-bar form from 60 BPM, in three levels: roots, a 1-2-3-5 pattern, arpeggios. Each level needs a successful loop.

pentatonic-scale.e3.name: Practice: A minor pentatonic
pentatonic-scale.e3.desc: Play the A minor pentatonic notes (frets 5–8) in the practice session with live scoring. Extra practice session — not required to pass the module.

major-scale.e3.name: Practice: C major scale
major-scale.e3.desc: Play the C major scale notes (frets 8–12) in the practice session with live scoring. Extra practice session — not required to pass the module.

melodic-minor.e3.name: Practice: A melodic minor
melodic-minor.e3.desc: Play the A melodic minor notes (frets 5–9) in the practice session with live scoring. Extra practice session — not required to pass the module.

harmonic-minor.e3.name: Practice: C harmonic minor
harmonic-minor.e3.desc: Play the C harmonic minor notes (frets 5–9) in the practice session with live scoring. Extra practice session — not required to pass the module.

pentatonic-scale.e4.name: Loop: improvise in box 1
pentatonic-scale.e4.desc: Improvise over Am7 (four bars) – Dm7 – Em7 using only the first pentatonic box (frets 5–8). 2 successful loops.

major-scale.e4.name: Loop: C major phrases
major-scale.e4.desc: Phrase with the C major scale over Cmaj7–Am7–Fmaj7–G7 and end your lines on C. 2 successful loops.

pentatonic-positions.e9.name: Build the box from a root
pentatonic-positions.e9.desc: You get one root G and the finger that holds it. Tap the rest of the box — six starting positions rebuild all five boxes. Extra practice.

pentatonic-positions.e7.name: Diagram: moving diagonally
pentatonic-positions.e7.desc: Three neighbouring boxes at once. The highlighted stack repeats an octave higher, so the same lick takes you diagonally across the neck. Extra practice.

pentatonic-positions.e8.name: Diagram: the pentatonic on one string
pentatonic-positions.e8.desc: The whole G minor pentatonic on the G string, from the open string to fret 12. It teaches the distances between notes instead of a box shape. Extra practice.

pentatonic-positions.e6.name: Loop: box to box
pentatonic-positions.e6.desc: Gm7–Cm7: move to a neighbouring pentatonic box with each loop. 2 successful loops.

modes.e4.name: Diagram: pentatonic + 2 notes = mode
modes.e4.desc: Every mode is a pentatonic from the same root with two notes added. The minor one gives Dorian, Aeolian and Phrygian; the major one gives Lydian, Ionian and Mixolydian. Extra practice.

modes.e5.name: Loop: pentatonic, then the mode
modes.e5.desc: One Dm7 chord for eight bars: first the pentatonic alone, then Dorian. Extra practice.

pentatonic-scale.e7.name: Loop: constraints
pentatonic-scale.e7.desc: Extra practice. Three variants: three notes only, one string only, a set rhythm. Fewer notes to choose from, more attention on rhythm and phrasing.

pentatonic-scale.e8.name: Loop: blues, minor and major
pentatonic-scale.e8.desc: Extra practice. Blues in A three ways: minor pentatonic, major pentatonic, and both in turn.

pentatonic-positions.e10.name: Loop: blues in G, minor and major
pentatonic-positions.e10.desc: Extra practice. Blues in G: minor pentatonic, major pentatonic, and both in turn. Move between the boxes as you play.

target-chord-tones.e5.name: Loop: approach notes
target-chord-tones.e5.desc: Extra practice. Approach the chord's root from a half step below, then surround it from above and below. The microphone checks the landing on beat one.

voice-leading.e4.name: Loop: approaching the thirds
voice-leading.e4.desc: Extra practice. Dm7–G7–Cmaj7: reach the third of each chord chromatically. The microphone checks the third on beat one.

modes.e6.name: Loop: modes from one root
modes.e6.desc: Extra practice. A chord on D keeps playing while the variant changes the mode: Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Mixolydian, Lydian.

modes.e3.name: Loop: modal colors
modes.e3.desc: Four variants (Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian). Emphasize the mode's characteristic note over each backing. 2 successful loops per variant.

chord-scale-major.e3.name: Loop: characteristic tones
chord-scale-major.e3.desc: Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 with a scale hint on each chord. Play the chord's characteristic tone at every change. 2 successful loops.

arpeggios.e3.name: Loop: arpeggios over ii–V–I
arpeggios.e3.desc: Dm7–G7–Cmaj7: play only chord arpeggios — no scale notes. 2 successful loops.

voice-leading.e3.name: Loop: thirds and sevenths in ii–V–I
voice-leading.e3.desc: Dm7–G7–Cmaj7: lead the thirds and sevenths (F→F→E, C→B→B). The mic checks thirds and sevenths.

switching-keys.e3.name: Loop: G major → B major
switching-keys.e3.desc: Halfway through the loop the key jumps a major third — move your scales and arpeggios to the new key.

chord-scale-melodic.e3.name: Loop: minor ii–V–i
chord-scale-melodic.e3.desc: Dm7b5–G7alt–Cm(maj7) or a single D7#11 — a scale hint on every chord.

melodic-minor.e4.name: Loop: Am6 – Am(maj7)
melodic-minor.e4.desc: Two shades of A minor: emphasize the 6 (F#) and the major 7 (G#). 2 successful loops.

harmonic-minor.e4.name: Loop: Am – E7
harmonic-minor.e4.desc: Over E7 emphasize G# — the characteristic note of A harmonic minor. 2 successful loops.

chord-scale-harmonic.e3.name: Loop: minor ii–V with harmonic minor
chord-scale-harmonic.e3.desc: Bm7b5–E7–Am: use Phrygian dominant over E7. 2 successful loops.

pentatonic-scale.e5.name: Loop: 12-bar blues
pentatonic-scale.e5.desc: 12-bar blues in A (A7–D7–E7). Improvise in pentatonic box 1. 2 successful loops.

target-chord-tones.e3.name: Loop: 12-bar blues
target-chord-tones.e3.desc: 12-bar blues in A — land on a chord tone at every change. 2 successful loops.

arpeggios.e4.name: Diagram: maj7 arpeggio
arpeggios.e4.desc: Cmaj7 arpeggio (1 3 5 7) across all strings, frets 7–11 — the I chord of the ii–V–I loop.

arpeggios.e5.name: Diagram: m7b5 arpeggio
arpeggios.e5.desc: Bm7b5 arpeggio (1 b3 b5 b7) across all strings, frets 7–11 — the vii chord of C major and the ii of a minor ii–V.

pentatonic-scale.e6.name: Loop: phrase and rest
pentatonic-scale.e6.desc: Extra practice. Am7–Am7–Dm7–Em7 in box 1: play a bar and rest a bar, or a two-bar question and a two-bar answer.

target-chord-tones.e4.name: Loop: phrase and rest
target-chord-tones.e4.desc: Extra practice. Am–C–Em–D: play a bar and rest a bar, or a two-bar question and a two-bar answer; end each phrase on a chord tone.
